116906088_a087f5e8.text: A fundamental goal in neuroscience is to uncover common principles by which different modalities of information are processed. In the mammalian brain, thalamus acts as the essential hub for forebrain circuits handling inputs from sensory, motor, limbic, and cognitive pathways. Whether thalamus imposes common transformations on each of these modalities is unknown. Molecular characterization offers a principled approach to revealing the organization of thalamus. Using near-comprehensive and projection- specific transcriptomic sequencing, we found that almost all thalamic nuclei fit into one of three profiles. These profiles lie on a single axis of genetic variance which is aligned with the mediolateral spatial axis of thalamus. Genes defining this axis of variance include receptors and ion channels, providing a systematic diversification of input/output transformations across the topography of thalamus. Single cell transcriptional profiling revealed graded heterogeneity within individual thalamic nuclei, demonstrating that a spectrum of cell types and potentially diverse input/output transforms exist within a given thalamic nucleus. Together, our data argue for an archetypal organization of pathways serving diverse input modalities, and provides a comprehensive organizational scheme for thalamus.

116906088_5a4a3480.text: We produced a near-comprehensive transcriptomic atlas of murine thalamus via microdissection of retrogradely labeled cells and subsequent RNAseq analysis (22 nuclei, 120 samples). Anterograde tracing of inputs to thalamus was used when identification of nuclear boundaries was ambiguous (Figure 1A,B for an example dissection approach). Labeled neurons from a given thalamic nucleus were pooled and profiled, an approach chosen because nuclear identity and projection target are major definers of cell type. See supplementary tables 1 and 2 for details on labelling strategies. To identify the relationship between the transcriptomes of thalamic nuclei in an unsupervised manner, we selected the top 500 most differentially expressed genes between thalamic nuclei (via an ANOVA-like test, see methods). Using this differentially expressed gene set, we grouped the thalamic nuclei via hierarchical clustering (1 -Spearman's correlation as distance metric), identifying five major subdivisions of nuclei (Figure 1C). We termed these profiles, not clusters, as we do not mean to imply discreteness between the classifications (see below). These profiles are not explained by the modality of information processed, since subnuclei of motor, somatosensory and visual complexes all split across different profiles. For example, the blue profile (Figure 1C) included both the cerebellar-recipient motor thalamus and the retina-recipient visual nucleus (lateral geniculate, LGd), whilst the red profile contained the basal ganglia recipient motor thalamus and the superior colliculus-recipient visual nucleus (lateral posterior, LP). Interestingly, the anterior dorsal nucleus (AD) and nucleus reuniens (RE) had distinct profiles and each formed profiles of their own. When schematic sections of thalamus were colored by these profiles, a mediolateral separation was observed, with the 'blue' nuclei being most lateral and 'yellow' nuclei most medial (Figure 1D). Thus, the largest fraction of linear gene expression variance in thalamus is not explained by modality, but rather a topographic axis spanning the structure's mediolateral extent.

Projection of single-cell data onto bulk principal component 1 (as in figure 2 Thus far we analyzed thalamic nuclei by pooling projection neurons from their anatomical position. The resulting transcriptional profiles could represent homogenous populations, discrete subtypes, or cells with graded differences. To probe these possibilities, we profiled the transcriptomes of individual neurons from motor, somatosensory, auditory, and prefrontal projection classes (supplementary table 3). Analysis of the single-cell RNAseq dataset resulted in multiple clusters for each projection class which, when projected onto the first principal component of our bulk RNAseq dataset, spanned the same axis of variance identified from bulk data (Figure 4 A,B,C, supplementary figure 4). Markers for this axis were spatially separated at the single-cell level, with clear intermediate cells present (Figure 4D, supplementary figure 5,6,7). However, some individual single-cell clusters had similar PC1 positions (e.g. clusters 1 and 2 of the motor projections neurons, or clusters 1 and 2 of the somatosensory nuclei, supplementary figure 4). This suggests that distinct clusters within a single modality could exist in similar anatomical positions. We examined this possibility by performing RNAscope for genes which distinguished these clusters (Pvalb and Tnnt1) . Using motor thalamus as an example, Pvalb and Tnnt1 expression were both found within the confines of a single thalamic nucleus, VL. While neurons selectively expressing each gene could be found, intermediate cells were also apparent. Pvalb-selective, intermediate, and Tnnt1-selective cells were distributed along the mediolateral axis (Figure 4E).

116906088_66839048.text: Therefore spatially organized genetic gradients can exist even within individual thalamic nuclei. In this study we produced a near-comprehensive transcriptomic atlas of thalamus via RNAseq in order to investigate its organizational structure. Though input modality has historically defined thalamic nuclei, several alternative, overlapping organizational classifications have been proposed 1,6 . Early work perturbing thalamus showed that nuclei of the same modality can have strikingly different contributions to behavior, leading to a division between arousal-linked intralaminar nuclei and the rest of thalamus [7][8][9] . More recently, theories developed in the sensory thalamus have subdivided thalamic nuclei into two groups, based upon anatomical or neurochemical features [10][11][12] . However, precise delineation of groups is not consistent between theories, and no theory is comprehensive. If and how these later theories apply beyond sensory thalamus, for example, is unknown. Here, we reconcile and extend these theories by placing almost all thalamic nuclei into one of three profiles, lying on a single topographic axis identified via unsupervised analysis. This axis extends from the midline/intralaminar groups through to a profile that includes the classic 'relay' sensory nuclei. Though prior theories did not incorporate electrophysiological properties, we found that genes directly affecting these properties were highly differentially expressed between groups, implying conserved, systematic variation of response properties across thalamus. Understanding how the pattern of intra-thalamic variability identified here is used to support different circuit functions will be an important challenge 13 . Prior theories of thalamic organization have placed thalamic cells into discrete nuclei, and thalamic nuclei into discrete groups. However, it remains unclear if subtypes of cells exist within nuclei and how discrete vs. continuous the cells type differences are. Recent studies in other non-thalamic areas have argued that gradients of projection neuron identities can exist 14,15 . Our single-cell transcriptomic data revealed heterogeneity within thalamic nuclei and suggest that thalamic genetic profiles exist on a spectrum, with mixtures of genetic profiles often existing in single neurons. Intermediate cell types exist both within and between nuclei, and are topographically localised.
